title: Sleep problems and insomnia
intro: Almost everyone has trouble sleeping at some point. Insomnia means persistent difficulty falling asleep, staying asleep or waking too early, together with tiredness or poor functioning during the day. Short-term problems usually pass, and for long-lasting insomnia, behavioural therapy works better and more durably than sleeping pills.

sections.heading: What insomnia is
paragraphs: Insomnia is diagnosed when problems occur at least three nights a week for a month or more and affect daytime functioning. Typical complaints are lying awake, waking in the night, early waking, unrefreshing sleep, fatigue, irritability and difficulty concentrating. Worry about sleep itself often keeps the problem going.

sections.heading: Causes and contributors
paragraphs: Stress, worry, changes in routine, shift work, pain, noise, caffeine, alcohol, nicotine and some medicines can disturb sleep. Insomnia often accompanies depression and anxiety. Other sleep disorders such as sleep apnoea and restless legs can cause poor sleep and should be checked if suspected.

sections.heading: Sleep habits that help
paragraphs: Keep regular bed and wake times, even on weekends, get daylight and exercise, and avoid caffeine in the afternoon and heavy meals or alcohol close to bedtime. Create a dark, quiet, cool bedroom, and reserve the bed for sleep. Avoid screens and stimulating activities late in the evening. If you cannot sleep after about twenty minutes, get up and do something relaxing until sleepy.

sections.heading: Treatment
paragraphs: Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia is the recommended first treatment. It includes sleep scheduling, limiting time in bed, changing unhelpful thoughts about sleep and relaxation. It can be delivered by a therapist, in groups or through approved digital programmes. Sleeping tablets can help in the short term but cause dependence, daytime drowsiness and falls, so they are used for short periods only. Herbal remedies such as valerian have uncertain benefit.

sections.heading: When to seek help
paragraphs: See a doctor if poor sleep persists for several weeks, if you snore loudly with pauses in breathing, fall asleep unintentionally during the day, or feel low or anxious. Do not drive when drowsy.

examples.title: Keeping a sleep diary
examples.text: Imagine you sleep badly most nights. You could record bedtime, wake times, naps, caffeine and mood for two weeks and bring the diary to your doctor.

examples.title: Breaking the worry cycle
examples.text: Suppose you lie awake worrying about tomorrow. You might write tomorrow's tasks on paper before bed and get up for a calm activity if you cannot sleep after twenty minutes.
